name: Jadidism
info: Jadidism was a Turco-Islamic modernist movement in the Russian Empire in the late 19th and early 20th century, which pressed for new-method schools, a Turkic-language press and Islamic reform until the Soviet purges of the 1920s and 1930s.

facts.where: The Russian Empire's Muslim and Turkic regions: Crimea, Tatarstan, Bashkortostan, the North Caucasus and Central Asia (Turkestan, Tashkent, Samarqand, Bukhara, Kokand), with echoes in Xinjiang.
facts.period: The first new-method school in Crimea (1884); new-method schools appearing in the last decade of the 19th century; a burst of Turkic newspapers after the 1905 Revolution until 1908; over 5,000 Jadid schools by 1916; the Kokand government (1917–1918); alliance with the Bolsheviks in the early 1920s; purges from 1926 through the 1920s and 1930s.
facts.figures: Ismail Gasprinsky (Gaspirali), Crimean Tatar educator and publisher; Mahmud Khoja Behbudiy, playwright and school founder; Abdurrauf Fitrat; Cholpan; Munawwar Qari; Sadriddin Ayni; Musa Bigiev; Ghabdennasir Qursawi; Zaynulla Rasulev.
facts.outcome: A network of new-method schools and a Turkic-language press, but no equality under Russian rule; the Kokand government was crushed in 1917–1918, and the Jadids were purged under Stalin. They have since been rehabilitated as national heroes in Uzbekistan.

t: The Jadids, who called themselves progressives, intellectuals or simply youth, held that Muslim peoples in Tsarist Russia had fallen into moral and societal decay that only a new kind of knowledge and European-modelled reform could cure.

Their signature was the Usul-i Jadid, the new method of teaching, which added geography, history, mathematics and science to the maktab curriculum, taught reading by phonetic methods and spread through schools and a Turkic-language press.
Their rivals were the Qadimist clergy and, after 1917, the Bolsheviks, who first used them and then purged them as counterrevolutionary agents; Uzbekistan has since honoured them as national heroes.
dyk: A Samarqand bookstore of 1914 sold books in Tatar, Ottoman, Arabic and Persian, along with dictionaries, atlases, maps and globes, according to the historian Adeeb Khalid.
ev: Ismail Gaspirali founds the first new-method school in Crimea
The 1905 Revolution opens a period in which Turkic-language newspapers appear in Turkestan; Russian authorities forbid them again in 1908
A school for training teachers in Jadid methods is founded in Turfan by Heyder Sayrani and the merchant Mukhsut Muhiti
Jadid-run institutions of learning number over 5,000
Jadids found a provisional government at Kokand, which the Tashkent Soviet crushes in 1918, killing around 14,000 people
The Communist Party in Central Asia turns on the Jadids in the same purges that struck the Ulama
Virtually the entire intelligentsia of Central Asia, including Cholpan and Abdurrauf Fitrat, is purged

sections.background:
The Jadid movement arose among the Turkic Muslim peoples of the Russian Empire in the late 19th century. Its members held that these peoples had entered a period of moral and societal decay. They saw the traditional maktab, the primary school, as the clearest sign of stagnation. Pupils memorised religious texts rather than having them explained: the Tajik Jadid Sadriddin Ayni, who attended a maktab in the 1890s, recalled that he learned the Arabic alphabet as an aid to memorisation but could not read a text he had not already memorised.

The Russian government offered an alternative. From 1884 it set up “Russo-native” schools in Turkestan, which combined Russian language and history with maktab-like instruction by native teachers, many of whom were Jadids. These schools reached too few people to bring the cultural renewal the Jadids wanted; in 1916 fewer than 300 Turks attended Russian higher primary schools in Central Asia.

Russian rule also kept the populations apart. Residence in Tashkent, the capital of Turkestan, was limited to Russian elites, and most cities had separate quarters for Russians and “natives”. New technologies of communication and transport, among them the telegraph, the printing press, the postal system and railways, carried Jadid ideals across Central Asia.
sections.aims:
The Jadids advocated an Islamic social and cultural reformation through the revival of pristine Islamic beliefs and teachings, while engaging with modernity. Education was a principal aim. They wanted schools that would teach differently from the maktabs, and held that the traditional system produced graduates without the skills to navigate the modern world. Their new-method schools, the Usul-i Jadid from which the name Jadidism derives, kept the traditional subjects and added geography, history, mathematics and science. Probably the most important change was teaching children to read by phonetic methods, which did more to encourage functional literacy.

Jadid schools focused on literacy in the native, often Turkic, languages rather than Russian or Arabic, taught “Islamic history and methods of thought” rather than memorisation alone, did not allow corporal punishment and encouraged girls to attend, although few parents sent their daughters. Some classrooms had benches, desks, blackboards and maps.

Jadids also criticised local society. Central Asian Jadids accused its leaders of permitting moral decay, as seen in alcoholism, pederasty, polygamy and gender discrimination, and of cooperating with Russian officials to cement their authority. Anti-colonial discourse was a major strand, and leaders such as Gasprinsky promoted anti-Russian political activism.
sections.events:
In 1884 Ismail Gaspirali founded the first new-method school in Crimea. Such schools quickly gained prominence among the Tatars, popularised by thinkers such as Ghabdennasir Qursawi, Musa Bigiev and Gaspirali himself, but spread to Central Asia more slowly and sporadically. Munawwar Qari founded Central Asia's first school on the Jadid model in Tashkent. Gasprinsky's newspaper Tercüman (“Interpreter”) was widely read in all Turkic regions of the empire. From 1905 to 1917, 166 new Tatar-language newspapers and magazines appeared. The first Turkic-language newspaper produced in Turkestan dates from after the 1905 revolution, and Central Asians published many papers until the Russian authorities forbade them again in 1908.

Russian electoral rules limited Jadid political power. After the 1905 October Manifesto, Turkestan's population was divided into “native” and “non-native” franchises, each sending one representative to the Duma, which gave the “non-native” franchise a two-thirds majority although it made up less than ten percent of the population. In 1913 a teacher-training institution in Jadid methods opened in Turfan. By 1916 Jadid-run institutions of learning numbered over 5,000.

After the October Revolution of 1917 the Jadids founded a unified provisional government at Kokand, intending to remain autonomous from the USSR. It lasted a year, 1917–1918, before the forces of the Tashkent Soviet brutally crushed it; around 14,000 people, including many leading Jadids, were killed in the ensuing massacre.
sections.people:
A leading figure in educational reform was the Crimean Tatar intellectual, educator, publisher and politician Ismail Gasprinsky (1851–1914). Mahmud Khoja Behbudiy, author of the play The Patricide and founder of one of Turkestan's first Jadid schools, carried Gasprinsky's ideas back to Central Asia. Among the Tatars, Ghabdennasir Qursawi and Musa Bigiev helped popularise the new schools, and the Bashkir leader Zaynulla Rasulev organised one of the first Jadid madrasahs. The Bukharan author Abdurrauf Fitrat criticised the clergy for discouraging the modernisation he thought necessary to protect Central Asia from Russian incursions, and the Tatar socialist Ismail Abidiy published newspapers in Central Asia.

Jadids had much in common with their opponents. Many were educated in traditional maktabs and madrasas and came from privileged families. Adeeb Khalid sees Jadids and the Qadimist Ulama as engaged in a battle over which values should be projected onto Central Asian culture. Many clergy opposed the Jadids, decrying their programmes as un-Islamic, heretical innovations, while Jadids called the Qadimists corrupt, self-interested elites. The Jadids also condemned Sufis as proponents of a popular, unorthodox form of Islam.

Jadids were not of one mind. In Xinjiang, Muhammad Amin Bughra and Masud Sabri rejected the name “Uyghur” for the Turkic people there, and some Turkmen opposed the single Turkestani language the Jadids proposed.
sections.outcomes:
The Jadids failed to achieve equality under Russian imperial rule in Turkestan. The Russians treated them better than the clergy, whom they regarded as dangerous extremists, because of the progressive and secular nature of their reforms, yet kept the idea that Turkestan's people should have separate living spaces and limited voting rights. Their papers in Central Asia usually had small circulations and needed patronage to survive, and the Russian censors saw them as potentially subversive.

The Bolsheviks at first offered state-funded schools, a print sphere immune to market forces and new organs of political authority, and by the early 1920s large numbers of Jadids joined the Communist Party. The Bolsheviks used these facilities on their own terms, for political education and propaganda. The Jadids hoped for a Turkic nation, while the Bolsheviks envisioned a Central Asia divided on ethnographic lines. The Bolsheviks then built local cadres bound to socialist revolutionism and cut off from Turkic cultural practice, who displaced the Jadids from public life.

By 1926 the Communist Party felt secure enough to act against traditional authorities without the Jadids, who were denounced as the mouthpiece of the local bourgeoisie and counterrevolutionary agents to be stripped of their jobs, arrested and executed if necessary. Through the 1920s and 1930s virtually the entire intelligentsia of Central Asia was purged, among them the writers Cholpan and Abdurrauf Fitrat.
sections.legacy:
Jadids have now been rehabilitated as “Uzbek National Heroes” in Uzbekistan, where they were recognised and honoured after the dissolution of the Soviet Union. Jadid-like schools were built by the Uyghur Progress Union of Kashgar after 1934, and Gasprinsky's example inspired figures such as Burhan Shahidi in Xinjiang. The Jadids popularised the identity of “Turkestani”, and Muhammad Geldiev, a Jadid, influenced the formulation of literary Turkmen, whose creation was assigned to a commission in 1921.

The movement carried an anti-colonial critique beyond Russia. After the defeat and collapse of the Ottoman Empire in the aftermath of World War I, the Jadids extended their critiques to Allied powers such as Britain and other Western European empires.

There were substantial ideological differences within the movement. Persian was the language of Jadidists in Central Asia at the start of the 1900s, and there was no broad scheme or ideology of pan-Turkism among them. Jadids normally referred to themselves by the Tatar terms Taraqqiparvarlar (“progressives”), Ziyalilar (“intellectuals”) or Yäşlär/Yoshlar (“youth”). What marked Jadids as a group was their widespread use of print media and their advocacy of the new method of teaching.

summary: Jadidism was a Turco-Islamic modernist movement among Muslims of the Russian Empire, built around new-method schools, a Turkic-language press and Islamic reform. Russian rule limited it, the Bolsheviks crushed its Kokand government in 1917–1918 and the Soviet purges removed its intelligentsia. Uzbekistan now honours its members as national heroes.
notes: The article gives no end year. The end is set at c. 1939 from 'throughout the remainder of the 1920s and 1930s' the intelligentsia was purged; start 1884 is the first new-method school, while the article also says Jadid-method schools appeared in the last decade of the 19th century.

The article names the movement 'Jadid movement' (title Jadid); 'Jadidism' is used as the article uses it. Spellings vary in the article: Gasprinsky, Gasprinskii, Gaspirali, Gasprinski; Behbudiy, Behbudi; Jadidist, Jadidists, Jadists.

The Central Asia section holds some oddly worded sentences (a Russian policy of enforcing traditional Islamic education 'to hamper and destroy opposition'; 'the policy of deliberately encouraging the neglect of culture and economy of the Turks'). Left out as the article gives no source or detail.

The article says Gasprinsky published satirical cartoons depicting clerics as rapacious and lustful; this is left out as a sensitive, thinly sourced detail. The Xinjiang material (Bughra, Sabri, Hui people, Artush school, Yunus Beg, First East Turkestan Republic) is mostly left out except as listed.

The 1916 figure of over 5,000 Jadid-run institutions is the article's; the 1884 date of the Russo-native schools and the 'less than 300' attendance figure are given as the article has them (in 1916 for the latter).
The 'North Caucasus' passage about Persian in Central Asia is placed oddly in the article; used only in the legacy section as the article states it.
The article says the Jadids 'embarked on language reform ... after 1917' and also that Muhammad Geldiev influenced literary Turkmen; the 1921 commission is the article's.
No references: the saved article's reference lists are empty; the 'Literature' section holds no entries.
